options: The average squared distance between a random variable's outcomes and its expectation value
The single most likely outcome of a measurement
The sum of all possible outcome values
The number of possible outcomes a distribution has
questions.explain: Variance is defined as Var[X] = sum of (x - E[X])^2 * P(x) -- it quantifies how spread out outcomes are around the mean, not the mean itself.

questions.q: Why does the variance formula square the distance from the mean instead of just averaging the raw distances?
options: Squaring makes every deviation positive, so distances in opposite directions don't cancel out, and it penalizes large deviations more heavily than small ones
Squaring is purely a mathematical convention with no real purpose
Squaring converts the result back into the original units automatically
Without squaring, variance would always equal zero
questions.explain: Raw (unsquared) deviations from the mean sum to zero by definition, which would make a 'raw average distance' meaningless -- squaring fixes this by making every term positive before averaging.

questions.q: What does standard deviation represent, as distinct from variance?
options: The square root of variance, which converts the value back into the same units as the original outcomes for direct interpretation
The same quantity as variance, just under a different name
The difference between the two most extreme possible outcomes
A probability value between 0 and 1
questions.explain: Variance is in squared units (hard to interpret directly); standard deviation undoes the squaring, giving a number directly comparable to the original outcome values.

questions.q: In the worked example (P(0)=0.64, P(1)=0.36), the standard deviation came out to 0.96 -- nearly as large as the maximum possible distance between +1 and -1. What does this indicate?
options: Even though the average leans toward +1, individual measurements still swing between both outcomes a lot, since 0.64/0.36 isn't that far from a 50/50 split
This result indicates an error, since standard deviation should always be much smaller than the range of possible values
It means every single measurement will return exactly the same outcome
It means the probabilities P(0) and P(1) were calculated incorrectly
questions.explain: A high standard deviation relative to the outcome range reflects genuine uncertainty in individual measurements -- here, the distribution isn't far from 50/50, so results really do vary a lot despite the mean leaning one way.

questions.q: Why does a measurement with higher variance require more shots to estimate its expectation value to the same precision as a lower-variance measurement?
options: The uncertainty in an averaged estimate scales as sigma/sqrt(N), so a larger single-measurement standard deviation (sigma) requires a larger N (more shots) to shrink the estimate's uncertainty to the same target level
Higher variance measurements are always physically impossible to run multiple times
Variance has no actual relationship to how many shots are needed
Lower variance always requires more shots, not fewer, than higher variance
questions.explain: The standard-error-of-the-mean formula (sigma/sqrt(N)) directly shows that a larger sigma needs a proportionally larger N to achieve the same final precision -- this is a real, practical shot-budgeting consideration.
